The electric bass is the **low voice** of a rock, jazz or pop band. It has four thick strings, frets like a guitar, and it is plugged into an **amplifier**. This page walks through the instrument and then gives you an interactive fretboard to learn where the notes are. Already a guitarist? [Bass for Guitarists](bass-for-guitarists.qmd) covers what changes in your hands.

## Where it came from {#history}

- The electric bass **descends from the acoustic double bass**, the largest and lowest of the bowed string instruments. The double bass played mostly in orchestras with a bow, and it was also the usual bass instrument in jazz and dance bands.
- Electric guitars began to be used in **1936**, and they were loud. Bands needed a bass that could keep up in volume.
- The first successful electric bass was built in the United States by **Leo Fender** and first sold in **1951**.
- It was louder, but it was also **smaller and easier to carry**, and easier to play accurately. Its body and neck were borrowed from the electric guitar, while its range and job stayed the same as the double bass's.
- **Monk Montgomery**, bassist with Lionel Hampton, was a pioneer of striking the strings with **downward thumb strokes**, which acted like the strong downward bow or finger strokes on the double bass.
- Today it is played in jazz groups, rock bands and other contemporary groups. Makers keep changing the wiring (**circuitry**) and the shapes of body and neck.

## Written higher than it sounds {#transposition}

The electric bass **sounds an octave lower than it is written**, as the double bass does. This keeps the music on the staff instead of down on a pile of ledger lines. Fingering fretboard notes and reading the staff are two different tasks: the chart below shows both, the **sounding** note you hear and the **written** note you read.

The four open strings sound **E1, A1, D2, G2** (middle C is C4). They are written **E2, A2, D3, G3** in the bass clef.

## The parts {#parts}

- **Body**: carries the **pickup** (a magnet that turns string vibration into an electrical signal), the **pickguard**, the **bridge** where the strings end, the **volume knobs** and **tone knob**, and the **output jack** where the cable plugs in.
- **Strap buttons**: one at the bottom of the body, one on the upper shoulder, for the strap.
- **Neck**: the **fingerboard** with its metal **frets**, from the **nut** (where the strings leave the headstock) down to the body. The first fret is the one nearest the nut.
- **Headstock**: holds the **tuners** (tuning pegs). On some basses all four are on one side, on others they are split on both sides.
- **Strings**: **E A D G**, thickest to thinnest.

## Amplifier, head and cabinet {#amp}

A bass needs an amplifier. A **combo** has the amp and the speaker in one box. A **head** (the amp alone) can be paired with a separate speaker **cabinet**, so you can pick a good head and upgrade the cabinet later. The book's points:

- **Impedance** is measured in ohms (Ω). Both heads and cabinets have a rating. The book's rule of thumb is that the head's rating should generally be **lower** than the cabinet's: a 4 Ω head into an 8 Ω cabinet is safe, but an 8 Ω head into a 4 Ω cabinet can overheat the head. (Check the amp's own manual before you connect anything. The rule is the book's, not checked here.)
- **Two cabinets**: in **series** the ohms add (8 + 8 = 16 Ω; safe, a bit less power). In **parallel** the formula is (A × B) ÷ (A + B), so two 8 Ω cabinets make 4 Ω, which uses a 4 Ω head to its full capacity.
- **Speaker size** changes the sound. Smaller speakers have more punch and midrange but give up low end. Larger ones have more low-mids and lows but can lose definition. More speakers add low end. Common cabinets: 2×10″ or 1×12″ (work for many styles), 1×15″ (good for rock, a bit muddy for concert or jazz band), 1×10″ (a little thin for electric bass).

## Setting up {#setup}

::: {.ebp-steps}
1. **Strap**: connect it to the strap buttons (bottom of the body, top left shoulder).
2. Put it over your shoulder and set it so the bass sits about at **belly-button height**, with the neck angled slightly **up**.
3. **Turn the amp volume down**, then plug the amp into a power outlet.
4. **Turn the volume on the bass down** too.
5. Cable: one end into the bass's **output jack**, the other into the amp's **input jack**.
6. Turn the amp on, then raise the volume on the amp and on the bass to a comfortable level.
:::

## Holding it {#posture}

1. **Always use a strap**, sitting or standing. Standing, the strap carries the full weight of the bass.
2. Sitting: **straight, on the front of the chair, feet flat**. Rest the curve of the body on your **right thigh** and the back of the bass against you.
3. Correctly held, the **thickest string (E) is closest to the ceiling** and the thinnest (G) closest to the floor.
4. **Left (fretting) hand**: grip the neck gently. The **thumb sits behind the neck at about the second fret**, pointing up with a slight curve.

## The two hands {#hands}

**Fretting hand.** The fingers are numbered **1 (index) to 4 (little finger)**. Press the string **all the way down** just **behind the fret** (on the nut side) for a clear tone. When two neighbouring strings are played at the same fret, the lower one is pressed with the **tip** of the finger and the higher one with the **pad**, so the finger rolls between them.

**Plucking hand.** Use the **index (i)** and **middle (m)** fingers, one after the other. The thumb rests on the **E string**, on the top edge of the **pickup**, or on the body. Pluck **upward**; to rest, the finger comes to the next lower-sounding string (to stop on the G, use the D string). Plucked open strings at normal volume should not buzz on the frets. Both fingers should sound the **same**.

**Where to pluck**: between the end of the fingerboard and the bridge. The tone is fuller further toward the neck and thinner toward the bridge (a general fact, not in the book).

## The fretboard {#fretboard}

Fretboard diagrams in the book stand the neck up with the headstock at the top and show the strings **E A D G** left to right. The one below lies on its side the way **tab** is written: the **G string on top**, **E at the bottom**. A dot on a fret means "press here"; "open" means the unfretted string. On the first four frets, **one finger per fret**: fret 1 with finger 1, fret 2 with finger 2, and so on (the book's chart does this).

Because the strings are tuned in fourths (E to A to D to G), each note a string higher is 5 frets **lower** on the next string: fret 5 of the E string is the same pitch as the open A string. That makes the same note available in several places.

### Find the note {#quiz}

You get a note and find it on the fretboard. In **staff** mode it must be exactly that pitch; in **name** mode any octave will do. Wrong clicks play the note you chose, so you learn what it was.

```{=html}
<div id="eb-quiz"></div>
```

## Tuning {#tuning}

In a group every instrument has to be in tune with the others. You tune by turning the **tuning pegs**: **loosen** a string to lower the pitch, **tighten** it to raise it. Press an open string and listen to the sound here:

```{=html}
<div id="eb-strings"></div>
```

With an **electronic tuner**:

1. Plug the bass's cable straight into the tuner's input and turn the tuner on.
2. Pluck an open string. The needle (or light) shows the note. Pointing **left** means **flat**: tighten. Pointing **right** means **sharp**: loosen.
3. Approach the note **from below**: if a string is sharp, first loosen it under the pitch, then tighten up to it. This keeps the tension steady.
4. In the middle of the dial (or a green light) the string is in tune. Do the **E, A, D and G** strings one at a time.
5. Always **double-check by ear** while playing with the band. A bass player must keep listening.

Another way to check by ear (not in the book): the note at **fret 5** of one string matches the next open string up. Play fret 5 of E, then open A; they should sound the same.

## Articulation {#articulation}

How a note starts (its **attack**) comes from the plucking fingers, **alternating i and m**. The strength of the pluck shapes the note. Aim for an **even sound** from both fingers. A note can ring on, or you can **mute** it: use the index or middle finger (usually the one that did not pluck) to stop the string.

## Tone problems {#tone-problems}

| What you hear | Probably because… | Try this |
|---|---|---|
| **No sound** | Amp not plugged in or not switched on | Check the amp plug and power switch |
| | Amp volume or bass volume turned down | Turn up both volume knobs |
| **Buzzing** | Fretting in the wrong place on the fret | Move the finger to just behind the fret |
| | Not enough pressure in the left hand | Press harder |
| **Crackling** | Bad cable or connector | Check both ends are pushed in; replace the cable |

## Check yourself {#checklist}

Have a friend or teacher check these: standing or sitting straight · shoulders relaxed · bass positioned right · right forearm and hand in the right place · right-hand fingers curved · left thumb behind the neck · left wrist straight, fingers arched · right hand between the end of the fingerboard and the bridge · plucking action correct · finger rests on the next string (or on the thumb after the E string) · index and middle make the same sound.

## Looking after it {#care}

After each practice: **turn the volume down** on the amp and the bass, switch the amp **off**, **unplug** the cable from both ends, **wipe the strings** with a soft cloth to remove dirt and oil, take off the strap and put the bass and strap in the case.

## Why start electric bass in a band? {#band}

For band directors, the book lists four reasons: it gives the band a solid bass voice and supports the tuba section; it supplies bassists for the jazz band, and some can move later to string bass (which advanced concert-band music uses); it gives a place in school music to students who aren't drawn to a traditional band instrument; and it can recruit low brass and woodwind players (a student could start tuba and electric bass at once, since some ideas carry over).
